title: Markets Under Painted Glass
subtitle: Kharadi society and visual identity
summary: Pale stone, turquoise and copper; cities learned by their routes; seals, ledgers and formal masks, and why a dishonest scale first cheats its owner.
content:
> *"A city is not its towers. A city is who trades with whom, and by which road."*
> — said of Kharadi cities

A Kharadi city is not something you take in from a viewpoint. It is something you learn by moving through it: by its routes, its courtyards, its covered markets and its bridges, and by who you know at the end of each of them. Kharadi visual identity is about **movement**, **wealth**, **layered exchange**, **craft**, **shade**, **negotiation** and **density**.

This entry describes how the [Kharad Compact](factions.html#kharad-compact) looks and how its people carry themselves. For its history, see [[the-kharad-compact|The Kharad Compact]]. For the faith behind its scales and seals, see [[covenant-of-the-one|The Covenant of the One]].

## Stone, Turquoise and Copper

The Kharadi palette is drawn from its materials: **pale stone**, **turquoise**, **deep blue**, **ivory**, **copper**, **bronze**, **burgundy**, **black** and **gold**, in patterned textiles, coloured glass, lacquer, dark wood and glazed ceramic.

The most common motifs are the **scales**, for justice and contracts; the **diamond**, often read as the unity of the cities; and **geometric order** of every kind. Kharadi sacred art never depicts the divine, and geometry, calligraphy and patterned light fill the spaces where other peoples would put images.

![The flag of the Kharad Compact](data/images/kharad-compact-flag-c402892f.jpg "The Kharadi flag: a balance set above stylised waves inside a measured ring, wreathed in laurel, on turquoise with copper-and-cream geometric borders and diamonds. Scales, diamonds and geometric trim recur on seals, sashes, banners and ledger cases.")

## Cities of Routes and Relationships

Kharadi cities are **dense** and built to be moved through: bazaars, courtyards, bridges, warehouses, banks, temples, shaded passages, domes, carved screens and water. Streets narrow into covered markets and open suddenly into courtyards with a fountain at the centre. Coloured glass throws patterns of light across stalls and floors. Most of all, the city is a network: it makes sense once you know which bridge leads to which market, and which market leads to which house.

![A Kharadi port city at the edge of the desert](data/images/kharad-compact-homeland-7134d104.jpg "A Kharadi port between desert and sea. Notice how much of the city is about movement: a camel caravan and a steam train crossing the same viaduct, glass-roofed market halls and cranes on the quays, ships of every size in the harbour, scales banners on the public buildings, and a masked envoy at work in the market in the foreground.")

> **A visitor's first afternoon in a Kharadi market, from a letter home**
>
> *I was told the copper market was "just past the fountain court". I found four fountain courts. Each one was just past another.*
>
> *By the third hour I had been offered tea eleven times, been sold a map of the market by a boy who then offered to guide me for the price of a second map, and passed the same seller of glass lamps three times from three different directions.*
>
> *When I finally sat down in despair, the lamp-seller brought me a cup of water, sat down beside me, and asked where I was trying to go. Then she walked me there, and would not take a coin for it. "You will remember the lamp-seller," she said, "and one day you will need a lamp."*
>
> *She was right. I bought two.*

## What Kharadis Wear

Kharadi clothing is shaped by heat, travel and trade: **layered, flowing garments**, **sashes**, **jewellery**, **patterned textiles** and loose, climate-appropriate cloth, with considerable variation from city to city. A well-dressed Kharadi looks cosmopolitan, carefully groomed and practically elegant, and their clothes quietly announce what they do and how well they do it.

![Kharadi clothing: commoner, merchant envoy, guard and Expeditioner](data/images/kharad-compact-clothing-dff706d8.jpg "Four Kharadis. A townsperson layered for heat, travel and city life, with useful pouches and tools for trade; a merchant envoy in luxurious but practical robes, carrying ledgers, seals and a formal mask; a guard in a disciplined uniform with civic insignia, who enforces contracts and keeps the peace; and an Expeditioner field-ready for deserts, coasts and new trade routes, with maps, survey tools and sample cases. Note the formal masks, the seal stamp and the ledger case, the backbone of trust.")

The objects people carry matter as much as the clothes. **Seals**, **ledgers** and **contract cases** travel everywhere with Kharadi merchants and envoys, because a seal makes an agreement real and a ledger keeps it honest.

## Masks

Kharad uses **formal masks** in certain settings: some commercial negotiations, auctions, diplomatic ceremonies and religious occasions. They are not everyday wear, and a Kharadi in a mask in the street would be as strange as an Aurelian in court dress at a fish market.

A mask represents the **role or institution** its wearer speaks for: a house, a bank, a guild, a city or an office. It separates the person from the obligation they currently represent. When a masked negotiator makes an offer, the offer comes from the house, not from them.

That is why **removing the mask** in the middle of a formal exchange means something. It says: *this has become personal.* Exactly how and when masks are worn varies between cities and occasions, and visitors are well advised to ask.

> **At a negotiation over salvage rights, from a clerk's notes**
>
> For two hours the masks spoke to each other in the formal register: the House offers, the House regrets, the House is unable to accept.
>
> Then the envoy across the table mentioned, almost in passing, the name of the crew that had died bringing the salvage home.
>
> Our envoy set her pen down. She untied her mask, laid it on the table between them, and looked at him with her own face.
>
> "No," she said. "This is not the House speaking now. My brother was on that crew."
>
> The other envoy was silent for a long time. Then, slowly, he untied his own mask and laid it beside hers.
>
> We had an agreement before evening.

## Reputation

The most important thing a Kharadi owns cannot be carried in a ledger case. It is their **reputation**, and Kharadi children learn early that it is worth more than any single deal.

> **A merchant and her apprentice, after closing**
>
> "He would never have known," said the apprentice. "The weights were close enough. We'd have made three times the margin."
>
> "On one sale." The merchant locked the strongbox. "And when he weighed it at home, as he would, he would tell his brother, and his brother's partners, and the guild. And every one of them would weigh everything we sold them for the next twenty years." She handed him the key. "A dishonest scale first cheats its owner. Qorvan said it. Your grandmother taught it to me. Now I'm teaching it to you, so I don't have to watch you learn it the expensive way."

## Machinery

Kharadi machinery is **modular**, **efficient** and **commercially practical**: easy to move, adapt, repair and resell. It is rarely plain. Decoration and utility sit comfortably together in Kharad, and a pump or a crane may carry geometric trim as carefully made as any carpet. Kharadi ships follow the same logic, built for cargo, range and modular fittings rather than display.

## What Foreigners Get Wrong

The laziest foreign stereotype of the Kharadi is greed. It misses nearly everything. Kharadis care about money, certainly, and they are very good with it. But what their culture actually prizes is **trust**, **reputation** and **correct measure**: deals that are fair enough to last, partners who will still deal with you tomorrow, and a scale that does not lie. A Kharadi who is only greedy is, by Kharadi standards, simply bad at business.
